learn: Living things share characteristics: they are made of cells, use energy, grow and develop, respond to their environment, reproduce and maintain stable internal conditions.
Keeping internal conditions stable is called homeostasis, like sweating to cool down.
Something must have all the characteristics to be considered alive.
check: All living things are made of...
Fire grows and uses energy. Is it alive?
No, it isn't made of cells
lessons.try: Decide whether fire, a seed and a crystal are alive, using the list.

learn: Living things need energy (food), water, living space and stable conditions.
Producers make their own food; consumers eat other organisms.
Most organisms need oxygen to release energy from food.
check: Organisms that make their own food are...
Most organisms need ___ to release energy.
lessons.try: List what a houseplant and a pet fish each need.

learn: Scientists classify organisms into groups based on shared traits.
Levels go from broad to specific: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Every species has a two-part scientific name, like Homo sapiens for humans.
lessons.try: Make a mnemonic to remember the classification levels.

learn: All living things are made of one or more cells.
Unicellular organisms (bacteria, amoebas) are one cell; multicellular organisms (trees, people) have many.
Cells are organised for specific jobs.
check: All living things are made of...
lessons.try: Compare an amoeba and a frog under the microscope (or images).

learn: Living things grow (get bigger) and develop (change form).
A tadpole develops into a frog.
Crystals grow but don't develop, and aren't alive.
check: A tadpole becoming a frog is...
lessons.try: Track a bean seed's growth over two weeks.

learn: Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two parents.
Asexual reproduction copies one parent (budding, splitting).
Reproduction continues species.
check: Sexual reproduction combines DNA from ___ parents.
lessons.try: Compare yeast budding and flower pollination.

learn: A stimulus is a change that causes a response.
Plants bend towards light; pupils shrink in bright light.
Responses help survival.
check: A plant bending to light is a...
lessons.try: Test how pill bugs respond to light and moisture.

learn: Organisms keep stable internal conditions.
Sweating cools you; shivering warms you.
Body temperature stays near 37 °C.
lessons.try: Measure pulse before and after exercise.

learn: All organisms need energy.
Producers make food; consumers eat.
Energy powers growth and movement.
lessons.try: Classify ten organisms as producers or consumers.

learn: Check all traits: cells, growth, reproduction, response, energy, homeostasis.
Fire grows and uses oxygen but isn't alive.
Viruses are a debated case.
check: To be alive, an organism shows ___ traits.
lessons.try: Debate five tricky examples.

learn: Biotic: living (plants, animals, fungi).
Abiotic: nonliving (water, sunlight, temperature).
Both shape ecosystems.
lessons.try: Survey biotic and abiotic factors in the schoolyard.

learn: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
Carl Linnaeus organised life in the 1700s.
Mnemonic: Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.
lessons.try: Classify a house cat all the way down.

learn: Binomial nomenclature: Genus species.
Humans: Homo sapiens. Wolves: Canis lupus.
Names are italicised; genus capitalised.
lessons.try: Look up scientific names of five animals.

learn: A key uses pairs of choices to identify organisms.
"Has feathers? Go to 2. No feathers? Go to 3."
Follow until you reach a name.
lessons.try: Use and then build a key for leaves.

learn: Traits of life.
Biotic and abiotic.
Classification and keys.
lessons.try: Classification card sort.

units.t: Cells: The Basic Unit of Life

learn: Cell theory states: all living things are made of cells, cells are the basic unit of life, and all cells come from existing cells.
Robert Hooke first named cells in 1665 after viewing cork under a microscope.
Anton van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see living single-celled organisms.
check: The basic unit of life is the...
lessons.try: Look at onion skin cells under a microscope or a photograph.

learn: Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria.
Plant cells also have a cell wall for support and chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
Plant cells often have one large central vacuole.
check: Which do only plant cells have?
lessons.try: Draw and label a plant cell and an animal cell side by side.

learn: The nucleus holds DNA and controls the cell.
Mitochondria release energy from food (the cell's powerhouse). Ribosomes make proteins.
The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves.
check: The "powerhouse" of the cell is the...
The control centre of the cell is the...
lessons.try: Compare a cell to a city: which organelle is the town hall, the power station?

learn: Light microscopes magnify up to about 1,000×.
Parts: eyepiece, objective, stage, focus knobs.
Start on low power.
check: Light microscopes magnify up to about...
lessons.try: Practise focusing on the letter "e".

learn: Robert Hooke named "cells" in 1665 looking at cork.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw living microbes.
Better tools brought discoveries.
lessons.try: Make a timeline of cell discoveries.

learn: All living things are made of cells.
Cells are the basic unit of life.
All cells come from existing cells.
check: The basic unit of life is the...
lessons.try: Write the cell theory in your own words.

learn: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus.
Eukaryotes (plants, animals, fungi) have a nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells are usually larger.
lessons.try: Compare the two cell types in a Venn diagram.

learn: The nucleus stores DNA, the cell's instructions.
DNA controls cell activities.
Chromosomes are coiled DNA.
lessons.try: Model DNA with a twisted ladder.

learn: The membrane controls what enters and leaves.
Plants have a rigid cell wall outside the membrane.
The wall gives support.
check: The membrane controls what ___ the cell.
lessons.try: Compare onion and cheek cells.

learn: Mitochondria release energy from food (cellular respiration).
They're the "powerhouse of the cell".
Muscle cells have many.
lessons.try: Explain why muscle cells need many mitochondria.

learn: Chloroplasts capture light for photosynthesis.
They contain green chlorophyll.
Found in plant cells, not animal cells.
lessons.try: Observe chloroplasts in an Elodea leaf.

learn: Ribosomes make proteins.
The endoplasmic reticulum transports materials.
The Golgi packages and ships proteins.
lessons.try: Model a cell as a factory.

learn: Vacuoles store water and waste; plants have one large central vacuole.
Lysosomes break down waste.
Wilting happens when vacuoles lose water.
lessons.try: Observe wilting and recovery in celery.

learn: Small cells have more surface area per volume.
That makes moving materials in and out efficient.
That's why big organisms have many small cells.
check: Small cells have ___ surface area per volume.
lessons.try: Compare agar cubes in dye.

learn: Microscopes and cell theory.
Prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
Organelles and their jobs.
lessons.try: Cell analogy project.

learn: Diffusion is the movement of particles from high concentration to low.
Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a membrane.
These are passive transport: they need no energy.
lessons.try: Put a drop of food colouring in still water and watch it spread.

learn: Active transport moves substances from low to high concentration.
It requires energy from the cell.
Cells use active transport to take in nutrients they need in large amounts.
check: Pushing a cart uphill is like...
lessons.try: Explain active transport using the idea of pushing a cart uphill.

learn: Cells divide so organisms can grow and repair damage.
Mitosis makes two identical cells with the same DNA.
The cell cycle includes growth, copying DNA and dividing.
check: Before dividing, a cell copies its...
lessons.try: Draw the stages of mitosis.

learn: Membranes let some things through and block others.
Small molecules like oxygen pass easily.
Large molecules need help.
lessons.try: Test a dialysis-tubing "cell" with starch and iodine.

learn: Particles move from high to low concentration.
No energy needed.
Oxygen diffuses into cells.
lessons.try: Watch dye diffuse in water.

learn: Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a membrane.
Water moves towards higher solute concentration.
A raisin swells in water.
lessons.try: Put potato slices in salt and fresh water.

learn: Facilitated diffusion uses protein channels.
Still high to low, still no energy.
Glucose enters some cells this way.
lessons.try: Diagram a protein channel.

learn: Moves particles from low to high concentration.
Requires energy (ATP).
Pumps keep cells balanced.
lessons.try: Compare passive and active transport.

learn: Endocytosis: membrane wraps around and brings in large items.
Exocytosis: vesicles release materials out.
White blood cells engulf bacteria.
lessons.try: Act out endocytosis with a hula hoop.

learn: Growth, repair and replacement.
Skin cells replace themselves constantly.
Single-celled organisms divide to reproduce.
lessons.try: List reasons cells divide in your body.

learn: Interphase (growth, DNA copying), mitosis, cytokinesis.
Most time is spent in interphase.
Checkpoints control the cycle.
lessons.try: Draw the cell cycle as a clock.

learn: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase (PMAT).
Chromosomes line up in metaphase; separate in anaphase.
Two identical nuclei result.
lessons.try: Order mitosis images.

learn: Meiosis makes sex cells (sperm and egg).
It halves the chromosome number.
Creates variety.
lessons.try: Compare mitosis and meiosis.

learn: Cancer is cells dividing out of control.
Damaged DNA can break checkpoints.
Sun protection and not smoking lower risk.
lessons.try: Research one way to reduce cancer risk.

learn: Passive and active transport.
Cell cycle and mitosis.
Meiosis and cancer.
lessons.try: Transport and division stations.

units.t: Levels of Organization and Body Systems

learn: Levels of organization: cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, organism.
A tissue is a group of similar cells. An organ is made of tissues working together.
The heart is an organ made of muscle, nerve and connective tissue.
check: A group of similar cells is a...
lessons.try: Make a diagram from cell to organism for the heart.

learn: The circulatory system (heart, blood, blood vessels) transports oxygen and nutrients.
The respiratory system (lungs, trachea) takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.
These systems work together: blood picks up oxygen in the lungs.
lessons.try: Measure breathing rate and pulse at rest and after exercise.

learn: The digestive system breaks food into nutrients.
The nervous system (brain, spinal cord, nerves) controls the body and processes information.
The skeletal and muscular systems support and move the body.
check: Food is broken down by the...
The brain is part of the...
Bones and muscles work together to...
lessons.try: Trace the path of food through the digestive system.

learn: Cells form tissues; tissues form organs; organs form systems.
Heart muscle cells → heart tissue → heart → circulatory system.
Systems form an organism.
lessons.try: Build a levels pyramid.

learn: Muscle, nerve, epithelial (covering), connective (bone, blood).
Each tissue has a job.
Plants have tissues too.
lessons.try: Match tissues to jobs.

learn: Four chambers: two atria, two ventricles.
The heart beats about 100,000 times a day.
Valves keep blood flowing one way.
check: The heart beats about ___ times a day.
lessons.try: Measure heart rate at rest and after exercise.

learn: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return it.
Capillaries exchange materials with cells.
Red cells carry oxygen; white cells fight germs; platelets clot.
lessons.try: Trace blood's path through the body.

learn: Air: nose → trachea → bronchi → lungs → alveoli.
Oxygen enters blood; CO₂ leaves.
The diaphragm powers breathing.
lessons.try: Build a model lung with a bottle and balloons.

learn: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine.
Enzymes break food into nutrients.
The small intestine absorbs most nutrients.
check: Most nutrients are absorbed in the...
Food goes from the mouth to the...
lessons.try: Model digestion with a bag and crackers.

learn: Brain, spinal cord and nerves.
Neurons send electrical signals.
Reflexes skip the brain for speed.
lessons.try: Test reaction time with a ruler drop.

learn: 206 bones support and protect.
Muscles pull on bones via tendons.
Joints allow movement.
lessons.try: Model a bicep and tricep with cardboard.

learn: Kidneys filter blood and make urine.
Skin and lungs also remove waste.
The immune system defends against germs.
lessons.try: Model kidney filtering with a sieve.

learn: Glands release hormones into blood.
Insulin controls blood sugar; adrenaline prepares for action.
Hormones act slowly but last.
lessons.try: Map major glands.

learn: Exercise: muscles need oxygen; heart and lungs speed up.
Nervous system coordinates.
No system works alone.
lessons.try: Map systems used in a sprint.

learn: Levels of organisation.
Major systems and organs.
Systems interact.
lessons.try: Body systems board game.

learn: Plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make glucose (sugar) and oxygen.
This happens in chloroplasts, which contain green chlorophyll.
Word equation: carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen.
lessons.try: Place a water plant in sunlight and watch for oxygen bubbles.

learn: Cells release energy from glucose using oxygen.
Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.
Respiration happens in mitochondria in both plants and animals.
lessons.try: Compare the two word equations and note how they are opposites.

learn: Photosynthesis and respiration form a cycle.
Plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen; animals do the reverse.
This balance helps keep the atmosphere stable.
lessons.try: Draw a diagram of the cycle with a plant and an animal.

learn: Photosynthesis turns light energy into chemical energy in sugar.
It happens in chloroplasts.
All food chains depend on it.
lessons.try: Diagram energy conversion in a leaf.

learn: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
Reactants: carbon dioxide, water. Products: glucose, oxygen.
Atoms are rearranged, not created.
lessons.try: Balance the equation with atom models.

learn: Light intensity, CO₂ level and temperature.
More light increases the rate up to a limit.
Too hot slows it.
check: More light ___ photosynthesis up to a limit.
lessons.try: Count Elodea bubbles at three light levels.

learn: Upper surface has many chloroplasts (palisade layer).
Stomata on the underside let gases in and out.
Guard cells open and close stomata.
check: Most stomata are on the leaf's...
lessons.try: Make a leaf peel and find stomata.

learn: Cells break down glucose with oxygen to release energy.
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (ATP).
Happens in mitochondria.
lessons.try: Compare the equations of photosynthesis and respiration.

learn: Breathing moves air in and out.
Cellular respiration happens in every cell.
Breathing supplies oxygen for respiration.
lessons.try: Explain the difference in a paragraph.

learn: Plants photosynthesise and respire.
At night, plants only respire.
Overall, they make more oxygen than they use.
check: Plants make ___ oxygen than they use.
lessons.try: Test CO₂ with bromothymol blue and plants in light and dark.

learn: Without oxygen, some cells use fermentation.
Yeast makes CO₂ and alcohol; muscles make lactic acid.
Releases less energy.
lessons.try: Inflate a balloon with yeast and sugar.

learn: Plants take in CO₂ and release O₂.
Animals take in O₂ and release CO₂.
The cycle balances gases.
lessons.try: Draw the cycle with arrows.

learn: Carbon is stored in forests, oceans, soil and fossil fuels.
Burning fuels releases stored carbon.
Forests are carbon sinks.
lessons.try: Map carbon stores.

learn: Food energy is measured in Calories.
All food energy began as sunlight.
Balanced diets fuel respiration.
lessons.try: Calculate Calories in a lunch.

learn: Opposite equations.
Chloroplasts and mitochondria.
Carbon-oxygen cycle.
lessons.try: Equation matching race.

learn: Heredity is passing traits from parents to offspring.
Genes are sections of DNA that carry instructions for traits.
Each parent gives one copy of each gene, so offspring get two versions (alleles).
check: Different versions of a gene are...
lessons.try: List inherited traits in your family, like eye colour.

learn: Gregor Mendel studied pea plants in the 1860s and discovered patterns of inheritance.
A dominant allele (T) hides a recessive allele (t).
Tt shows the dominant trait; tt shows the recessive trait.
check: A recessive trait shows only when...
lessons.try: Find which pea traits Mendel studied.

learn: A Punnett square predicts possible offspring.
Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt: a 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive.
Probabilities: 75% dominant, 25% recessive.
check: Tt × Tt: chance of tt is...
Tt × tt: chance of Tt is...
lessons.try: Make a Punnett square for Tt × tt.

learn: Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to offspring.
Inherited traits: eye colour, blood type. Acquired traits: scars, skills.
Only inherited traits pass through genes.
lessons.try: Sort twenty traits into inherited and acquired.

learn: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a trait.
Alleles are different versions of a gene.
You inherit one allele from each parent.
check: Different versions of a gene are...
You get one allele from each...
A gene is a section of...
lessons.try: Model alleles with coloured beads.

learn: Mendel crossed pea plants in the 1860s.
Tall × short gave all tall offspring; the next generation was 3 tall : 1 short.
He discovered dominant and recessive factors.
lessons.try: Analyse Mendel's data.

learn: A dominant allele (T) shows when present.
A recessive allele (t) shows only when two are present (tt).
Capital letters for dominant.
lessons.try: Predict traits from allele pairs.

learn: Genotype is the allele pair (TT, Tt, tt).
Phenotype is the visible trait (tall, short).
Homozygous: same alleles; heterozygous: different.
lessons.try: Label genotypes and phenotypes.

learn: A grid shows possible offspring.
Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt: 3 tall : 1 short.
Each box is a 25% chance.
check: Tt × Tt gives ___ chance of tt.
lessons.try: Complete five Punnett squares.

learn: Tt × tt: 50% Tt, 50% tt.
Each child is an independent event.
Actual families can differ from predictions.
lessons.try: Flip coins to simulate offspring.

learn: Incomplete dominance: red × white snapdragons → pink.
Codominance: both show, like red and white spotted cattle.
Not all traits are simple.
check: AB blood type is an example of...
lessons.try: Predict snapdragon colours.

learn: Some traits depend on many genes: height, skin colour.
They show a range, not just two forms.
Environment also matters.
lessons.try: Graph the heights of the class.

learn: A mutation is a change in DNA.
Can be harmful, helpful or neutral.
Some cause genetic disorders.
check: A mutation is a change in...
lessons.try: Research a genetic disorder.

learn: Family trees track traits over generations.
Squares are males; circles are females; shaded = has trait.
Pedigrees reveal recessive patterns.
lessons.try: Read a pedigree for a family trait.

learn: Genes, alleles, dominance.
Punnett squares and probability.
Mutations and pedigrees.
lessons.try: Genetics challenge cards.

learn: Individuals in a species vary in their traits.
An adaptation is a trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
Examples: a polar bear's thick fur, a cactus's spines.
check: A trait that helps survival is an...
lessons.try: Describe three adaptations of an animal in a cold climate.

learn: Charles Darwin described natural selection in "On the Origin of Species" (1859).
Organisms with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, passing those traits on.
Over many generations, populations change.
check: Helpful traits become ___ common over time.
lessons.try: Model natural selection with coloured paper "moths" on different backgrounds.

learn: Fossils show how life has changed over time.
Similar bone structures in different animals (like arms, wings and flippers) suggest common ancestry.
DNA comparisons show how closely species are related.
check: Similar bones in different species suggest...
DNA comparisons show how ___ species are.
lessons.try: Compare the bones of a human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper.

learn: Individuals of a species differ.
Variation comes from genes and mutations.
Variation is the raw material of evolution.
check: Variation is the raw material of...
lessons.try: Measure variation in sunflower seeds.

learn: Adaptations are traits that help survival and reproduction.
Cactus spines, owl hearing, camouflage.
Structural, behavioural or physiological.
check: A cactus spine is a ___ adaptation.
lessons.try: Classify ten adaptations.

learn: Charles Darwin sailed on HMS Beagle (1831–36).
Finches on different islands had different beaks.
Beaks matched food sources.
lessons.try: Match finch beaks to foods.

learn: More offspring are born than survive.
Individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more.
Over generations, helpful traits become common.
check: Survival of the ___ means best suited.
lessons.try: Simulate selection with bird-beak tools.

learn: Before factories, light moths blended on light trees.
Soot darkened trees; dark moths survived more.
When pollution fell, light moths returned.
lessons.try: Graph moth populations over time.

learn: Antibiotics kill most bacteria, but resistant ones survive.
Survivors reproduce; resistance spreads.
Finish prescribed courses; don't overuse.
lessons.try: Model resistance with beans.

learn: Humans choose traits to breed: dog breeds, crops.
Corn came from teosinte, a wild grass.
Faster than natural selection.
lessons.try: Compare teosinte and corn.

learn: Fossils show life changed over time.
Transitional fossils like Tiktaalik link fish and land animals.
Older layers hold simpler life.
lessons.try: Arrange fossils in order.

learn: Homologous structures share origins: human arm, bat wing, whale flipper.
Vestigial structures have lost function: whale hip bones.
Similar structures suggest common ancestry.
check: A bat wing and human arm are...
lessons.try: Compare limb bones of four animals.

learn: Early embryos of vertebrates look similar.
DNA comparisons show relationships.
Humans and chimpanzees share about 98% of DNA.
check: Humans and chimps share about ___ of DNA.
lessons.try: Compare DNA similarity percentages.

learn: Isolated populations can become new species.
Different environments select different traits.
Grand Canyon squirrels: Kaibab and Abert's.
check: Kaibab and Abert's squirrels were separated by the...
lessons.try: Map how isolation creates species.

learn: Variation and adaptation.
Natural and artificial selection.
Fossil, anatomical and DNA evidence.
check: Bat wings and human arms are...
lessons.try: Evolution evidence gallery.

learn: Bacteria are single-celled organisms without a nucleus.
Most bacteria are helpful: they help digest food and recycle nutrients.
Some bacteria cause illnesses; antibiotics can treat bacterial infections.
check: Bacterial infections can be treated with...
lessons.try: List three helpful uses of bacteria.

learn: Viruses are not cells. They need a host cell to make copies of themselves.
Colds and flu are caused by viruses.
Antibiotics do not work on viruses; vaccines help prevent many viral diseases.
check: Antibiotics work on viruses. True or false?
lessons.try: Make a chart comparing bacteria and viruses.

learn: The immune system defends the body against germs.
White blood cells attack invaders and remember them.
Hand washing, sleep and good nutrition support immunity.
lessons.try: Make a poster on preventing the spread of germs.

learn: Microorganisms are too small to see without a microscope.
Bacteria, protists, some fungi.
Most are harmless or helpful.
lessons.try: Observe pond water microbes.

learn: Shapes: cocci (spheres), bacilli (rods), spirilla (spirals).
No nucleus; some have flagella.
They reproduce by binary fission.
lessons.try: Draw the three shapes.

learn: Gut bacteria help digestion.
Bacteria make yoghurt and cheese.
Decomposers recycle nutrients.
lessons.try: Make yoghurt and observe.

learn: Some cause disease: strep throat, food poisoning.
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections.
Handwashing and cooking food prevent spread.
lessons.try: Test handwashing with glitter "germs".

learn: Protists include amoebas, algae and paramecia.
Fungi include moulds, yeasts and mushrooms.

lessons.try: Grow bread mould safely in a sealed bag.

learn: Viruses are tiny particles of DNA or RNA in a protein coat.
They can only reproduce inside a host cell.
Not considered fully alive.
lessons.try: Build a virus model.

learn: Droplets, touch, blood, insects.
Colds and flu spread through droplets.
Covering coughs reduces spread.
lessons.try: Model droplet spread with a spray bottle.

learn: Skin and mucus are the first barriers.
White blood cells attack invaders.
Antibodies tag specific germs.
lessons.try: Act out an immune response.

learn: Vaccines train the immune system safely.
Edward Jenner made the first vaccine (smallpox, 1796).
Smallpox was eradicated in 1980.
lessons.try: Make a vaccine history timeline.

learn: An epidemic spreads widely in a region; a pandemic spreads worldwide.
Public health measures: clean water, vaccines, sanitation.
John Snow traced cholera to a water pump in 1854.
check: John Snow traced cholera to a...
lessons.try: Analyse Snow's cholera map.

learn: Sleep, nutrition, exercise and hygiene support immunity.
Teens need about 9 hours of sleep.
Balanced meals with fruit and vegetables.
check: Teens need about ___ hours of sleep.
lessons.try: Plan a healthy week.

learn: Bacteria, protists, fungi and viruses.
Disease spread and defences.
Vaccines and public health.
lessons.try: Microbe trading cards.

learn: An ecosystem includes living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts.
Biotic: plants, animals, fungi. Abiotic: sunlight, water, soil, temperature.
A population is one species in an area; a community is all species in an area.
check: All species in an area form a...
lessons.try: List the biotic and abiotic parts of a pond.

learn: Energy flows from producers to consumers to decomposers.
Herbivores eat plants; carnivores eat animals; omnivores eat both.
Food webs show many connected food chains.
check: An animal that eats both plants and animals is an...
lessons.try: Draw a food web for a forest with at least eight organisms.

learn: Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next.
The rest is used for life processes or lost as heat.
That is why there are fewer top predators than plants.
check: About ___ of energy passes to the next level.
Starting with 10,000 units, the next level gets...
There are fewer top predators because...
lessons.try: Draw an energy pyramid starting with 10,000 units of energy.

learn: Organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome, biosphere.
A population is one species in an area.
A community is all populations in an area.
check: All the deer in a forest form a...
All living things in an area form a...
lessons.try: Build a levels-of-ecology diagram.

learn: A habitat is where an organism lives.

check: Two species ___ share the exact same niche for long.
lessons.try: Describe the niche of a desert animal.

learn: Food, water, space and shelter limit populations.
Carrying capacity is the maximum an area supports.
Populations rise and fall around it.
check: The most an area supports is its carrying...
lessons.try: Graph a population reaching carrying capacity.

learn: Primary consumers eat producers.
Secondary consumers eat primary consumers.
Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers.
check: A grasshopper eating grass is a ___ consumer.
A frog eating a grasshopper is a ___ consumer.
A hawk eating a snake (that ate a frog) is...
lessons.try: Label consumers in a food chain.

learn: Webs show many feeding links.
Removing one species affects many.
Keystone species have huge effects (sea otters).
lessons.try: Remove a species from a web and predict effects.

learn: About 10% of energy passes to the next level.
10,000 J in grass → 1,000 J in grasshoppers → 100 J in frogs.
Fewer organisms at top levels.
check: 10,000 J at producers → ___ J at primary consumers
1,000 J → ___ J at the next level
lessons.try: Calculate energy at each level.

learn: Biomass is total mass of living matter at each level.

check: Biomass is total ___ of living matter.
lessons.try: Compare biomass pyramids.

learn: Desert, grassland, tundra, taiga, temperate forest, rainforest.

Arizona has desert, grassland and forest.
lessons.try: Map biomes on a world map.

learn: Freshwater: lakes, rivers, wetlands.
Marine: oceans, coral reefs, estuaries.

lessons.try: Compare a pond and a coral reef.

learn: Primary succession starts on bare rock (lichens first).

Ecosystems change over time.
check: After a fire with soil left:
lessons.try: Sequence succession pictures.

learn: Quadrats count organisms in a square.
